blocks.text: In third place I count those for whom אנקה anaka is a kind of lizard; they are neither few nor to be despised. For in the Syriac we read ܐܡܩܬܐ amaktha, or amkatha, which the most learned of the Maronites, the late Gabriel Sionita (ὁ μακαρίτης [ho makaritēs]), rendered lacerta [lizard]. In the Samaritan it is [?] semamitha, that is, stellio, as will become clear in its proper place. In Erpenianus it is الورل [al-waral] alvvarlo, that is, a species of lizard which the barbarous writers call guaril. In the Arabic edition published at Paris it is الورك [al-warak] alvvarco, which is the same thing [II, 489]. For by what chance I do not know, in Avicenna and others الورك [al-warak] alvvarco is written far more often, although the true spelling is الورل [al-waral] alvvarlo. This is taught by all the Arabic lexicographers, and the barbarous name guaril is derived from it. Not to mention the critical observation which is found in Damiri, in the chapter ورل [waral] Guaril: لا تلتقي الراء مع اللام الا في اربع مواضع الورل وهو الحيوان المذكور وارل اسم جبل والغرلة وهو القلفة وحرل وهو ضرب من الحجارة [lā taltaqī al-rāʾ maʿa al-lām illā fī arbaʿ mawāḍiʿ al-waral wa-huwa al-ḥayawān al-madhkūr wa-aral ism jabal wa-al-ghurla wa-hiya al-qulfa wa-ḥaral wa-huwa ḍarb min al-ḥijāra]. Re does not meet with Lam (that is, R with L) except in four places. 1. In alvvarlo, the name of the animal discussed above. 2. In Aral, the name of a mountain discussed above. 3. In alghorla, which means foreskin (like the Hebrew ערלה). 4. In charal, which is a kind of stone. These, then, are the four ancient versions, the Syriac, the Samaritan and the two Arabic, for which anaka is a species of lizard. I have weighty reasons for casting my vote with them. 1. צב tsab, that is, the land crocodile, had preceded, and four other species of lizards are added immediately afterwards [col. 1066], as will be evident from what follows. Accordingly anaka seems to belong to the same genus. For the mygale, or any other animal, would be inserted rather inappropriately among so many species of lizards. 2. The Syriac ܐܡܩܬܐ amaktha, or amkatha, plainly arose from the Hebrew אנקה anaka. For these two words (apart from the ending, which is Hebrew in the one and Syriac in the other) differ in no respect, except that the Syrians changed the Hebrew NUN into MEM, a change than which nothing is more frequent in those languages. Thus among the Chaldeans or Syrians strong is ܚܣܝܢ chasin and ܚܣܝܡ chasim; reason, ܛܥܢܐ taana and ܛܥܡܐ taama; nymph, ܢܝܢܦܐ ninphe and ܢܝܡܦܐ nimphe; cudgel, ܩܘܪܢܣܐ kurnesa and ܩܘܪܡܙܐ kurmeza; the terebinth, or the tree that bears the pistachio, ܒܘܛܡܐ butem, as in Hebrew בוטן boten. And in Arabic thumb is ابهام [ibhām] ibham for the Hebrew בהן bohen; likewise to grow fat, دسم [dasama] dasama, for the Hebrew דשן dasen; and to sing, رنم [ranima] ranima, for the Hebrew רנן ranan. In Ethiopic ዘመወ፡ zamavva, he committed fornication, for the Hebrew זנה zana; እድሜ፡ edem, time, for the Chaldee עדן iddan; አደመ፡ adam, pleasant, sweet, from the Hebrew עדן adan, to take delight. Of the same kind is the Egyptian ΜΕΤΩΠΟΝ [metōpon], a kind of ointment, from the Hebrew נטף nataph or the Chaldee נטופא netopha; and ΜΕΙΣΙ [meisi], serpent, from the Hebrew נחש naas. So too the Egyptian city of Memphis is called by the Prophets now נוף Noph, now מוף Moph. By a like example the Syriac ܐܡܩܬܐ amaktha is here derived from the Hebrew אנקה anaka, with N and M interchanged. Therefore, whatever the Syriac amaktha may be, it is highly probable that the Hebrew anaka is the very same. Now it is certain that ܐܡܩܬܐ is a kind of lizard, and indeed the stellio, Prov. XXX, 28, where it stands in the Syriac [II, 490] Paraphrase for the Hebrew שממית semamith; just as in the Chaldee, by metathesis (μετάθεσιν [metathesin]) of the letters, אקמתא akmetha, which is the same. Therefore, as the Syriac ܐܡܩܬܐ amaktha, or amkatha, and the Chaldee אקמתא akmetha is the stellio, so also is the Hebrew אנקה anaka. Hence it is that the Samaritan too renders אנקה anaka by * [?] semamitha, that is, stellio; and both Arabic versions by الورل [al-waral] alvvarlo, or الورك [al-warak] alvvarco, a kind of lizard close to the stellio, which many therefore take for the stellio, because it is similar in form. Accordingly Alkazuinius says of it: هو العظيم من شكل الوزغ وسوام ابرص [huwa al-ʿaẓīm min shakl al-wazagh wa-sawām abraṣ] It is a large one, of the same form as the guezga and savvamabras, that is, as the smaller and larger stellios. This is taken from Avicenna. And Alcamus: الورل دابة كالضب والعظيم من اشكال الوزغ [al-waral dābba ka-al-ḍabb wa-al-ʿaẓīm min ashkāl al-wazagh] Alvvarlo (commonly guaril), an animal like the dhab (or land crocodile). And it is the large one among those which have the form of the guezga, or stellio. 3. In Hebrew אנקה anaka means a groan and a shrill cry, such as is uttered in great mourning. If anyone should deny that the stellio can be so called, as though it were a mute animal, he will be refuted by these words of Pliny on the stellio of Greece, book 29, chapter 4: The Greeks call it colotes, and ascalabotes, and galeotes. It does not occur in Italy. For it is covered with spots, has a harsh shriek, and feeds on *. All of which is foreign to our stellios. Note: a harsh shriek. In Greek you would say τρισμοῦ τραχέος [trismou tracheos], whence it is rightly called אנקה anaka. And as among the Hebrews a masculine plural is often formed from a feminine singular, as [col. 1067] יעלים from יעלה, and יענים from יענה, so from אנקה anaka the plural could be אנקים. And in the second Targum of Esther, chapter 1, verse 2, where among the various animals which each utter their own cry before Solomon are described אנקין בכיין anakin weeping, or wailing, this should perhaps be understood not (as it is commonly taken) of the screaming of eagles, but of the cry and harsh shriek of stellios, which the very word אנקה anaka attests approaches wailing. And for this very reason the Arabs, since they knew at least this much, that the anaka is a kind of lizard, rendered it الورل [al-waral] alvvarlo, which itself also has a voice, though perhaps less resonant. Hence Alcamus: ضغث الورل صوت [ḍaghatha al-waral ṣawt] Dhagathsa alvvarlo, that is, it cried out. This those of our scholars who have published Arabic lexicons did not sufficiently understand. For one rendered it The thigh made a cracking noise; another, The hip sounded. For they read الورك [al-warak] alvvarco, which means ירך, i.e. hip. But they ought to have remembered that this very الورك [al-warak] occurs everywhere for الورل [al-waral], as we noted above ^{d)}. Not to mention that in the copy of Alcamus which I used, الورل [al-waral] alvvarlo is quite correctly written. Therefore, what has hitherto escaped our scholars, let this stand as [II, 491] established: that among the lizards some are vocal, and among them is the stellio, which shrieks very shrilly. But we shall say more about the stellio in the explanation of the word שממית semamith.
